mean: (of a worry) to turn out groundless
lit: to end as the worry of the man of Qi: a fear that the sky might fall

story.text: A man of the small state of Qi was so afraid that the sky would fall and the earth would give way that he could neither sleep nor eat. Someone went to reassure him, explaining that the sky is only gathered air and the earth only piled-up soil, so there is nothing to collapse, and the man was greatly relieved. His needless fear, 'the worry of the man of Qi', gave Japanese the word kiyū.

use.how: Subject is a worry or fear, looked back on: 心配は杞憂に終わった. Also as a hope: 杞憂に終わればいいが (I hope my worry proves groundless).

near.diff: 取り越し苦労 is the act of worrying ahead of time; 杞憂に終わる reports that such a worry turned out to be unfounded.
胸をなで下ろす is the relief a person feels; 杞憂に終わる says the feared thing never happened.

mean: a gateway to success in a field
lit: climbing the Dragon Gate: the rapids that turn a carp into a dragon

story.text: The Dragon Gate (ryūmon) was a stretch of violent rapids on the Yellow River. It was said that great fish gathered below it but few could swim up, and one that did turned into a dragon (in Japan the fish is told as a carp). In the Later Han, being received by the respected official Li Ying was so great an honour that people called it 'climbing the Dragon Gate'. Hence a hard test whose passing opens the way to success.

use.how: Noun, usually in AはBの登竜門だ, where A is a contest, award or exam and B a career: 新人作家の登竜門. Not used of people.

near.diff: 関門 is any barrier to get through; 登竜門 is a test whose passing launches a career or brings recognition.
白羽の矢が立つ is being picked out by others; 登竜門 is the contest or test through which one makes one's name.

mean: to incur the wrath of a superior
lit: to touch the reversed scale under a dragon's throat

story.text: Han Feizi wrote that a dragon is gentle enough to be tamed and ridden, but under its throat grows one scale, a foot across, that lies the wrong way. Anyone who touches it is killed. mean: the heart-wrenching pain of a hard choice
lit: a feeling like one's bowels being torn apart

story.text: When the general Huan Wen was sailing through the Three Gorges, one of his men caught a baby monkey. mean: the crucial moment, the moment of truth
lit: the scene where one's true self must show

story.text: In kabuki and jōruri puppet theatre, the shōnenba (also written with the characters for 'true nature scene') was the most important scene of a role, where the lead actor had to bring out the true nature of the character. From the theatre the word spread to mean any crucial point where a person must show what they are made of.

near.diff: 土壇場 is the last moment with no time left, often with a sudden reversal; 正念場 is the decisive stretch where you must hold firm and give everything.
大詰め is simply the final stage of a process; 正念場 stresses that this is the make-or-break test of one's strength.

lit: the earth mound of the execution ground

story.text: In the Edo period, beheadings were carried out on a dotan, a mound of piled earth built at the execution ground, and the place was called the dotanba. Since a person brought there had no way out, the word came to mean the very last moment, when nothing more can be done.

use.how: Noun, mostly 土壇場で (at the last moment) with a reversal, cancellation or change: 土壇場で逆転した, 土壇場になって断られた. Also 土壇場に追い込まれる.

大詰め is the closing stage of a process, calm and planned; 土壇場 is the desperate last moment, often with a surprise.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は何[なに]をするかわからない{番狂[ばんくる]わせ}な人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he is an unpredictable person)
bad.why: It names an unexpected result, not a personality, and it never takes na. Say yosoku dekinai hito.

mean: to hold one's own against anyone
lit: not to take a retreat: not to fall back before a rival

use.how: Predicate: AはBに(も)引けを取らない, A is no worse than B. Also 誰にも引けを取らない, プロにも引けを取らない腕前. Praises skill or quality.

near.diff: 肩を並べる says someone has reached the same rank as another; 引けを取らない says they are not inferior when compared, often against a stronger rival.

cue: A home cook's ramen is so good that, tasting it side by side with a famous shop's, nobody can say which is better.

ctx.s: 母[はは]の料理[りょうり]はレストランにも{引[ひ]けを取[と]らない}。
ctx.en: My mother's cooking is every bit as good as a restaurant's.

ctx.s: 「この町[まち]の祭[まつ]りって有名[ゆうめい]なの？」「規模[きぼ]では京都[きょうと]にも{引[ひ]けを取[と]らない}よ。」
ctx.en: "Is this town's festival famous?" "In size it's a match even for Kyoto's."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は英語力[えいごりょく]なら誰[だれ]にも{引[ひ]けを取[と]らない}。
ctx.en: When it comes to English, he can hold his own against anyone.

ctx.s: 国産[こくさん]のワインも、今[いま]では海外[かいがい]の名品[めいひん]に{引[ひ]けを取[と]らない}品質[ひんしつ]だ。
ctx.en: Domestic wine is now of a quality that stands comparison with famous foreign labels.

ctx.s: 体[からだ]は小[ちい]さいが、パワーでは大柄[おおがら]な選手[せんしゅ]に{引[ひ]けを取[と]らなかった}。
ctx.en: He was small, but in power he was a match for the big players.

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]ながら、彼女[かのじょ]の企画[きかく]はベテランに{引[ひ]けを取[と]らない}出来[でき]だった。
ctx.en: Though she was new, her proposal was the equal of anything the veterans produced.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の歌[うた]は誰[だれ]にも{引[ひ]けを取[と]らない}ほど下手[へた]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he sings worse than anyone)
bad.why: It praises being as good as the best. It cannot be used for being the worst at something.

bad.s: 新人[しんじん]だから、先輩[せんぱい]たちに{引[ひ]けを取[と]らない}のは当然[とうぜん]だ。
bad.en: (meant: as a newcomer, it's natural to fall short of the seniors)
bad.why: The negative form means NOT inferior. For falling short say senpai-tachi ni oyobanai or kanawanai.

r: うしろがみをひかれる
lit: to feel as if the hair at the back of your head is being pulled as you walk away

use.how: Mostly 後ろ髪を引かれる思いで + leaving: 後ろ髪を引かれる思いで家を出た. Said at the moment of leaving a person or place you do not want to leave.

near.diff: 名残惜しい is sorrow that a pleasant time is ending; 後ろ髪を引かれる is the pull you feel as you actually walk away, often from someone who needs you.
断腸の思い is agony over a hard decision; 後ろ髪を引かれる is a lighter, lingering reluctance in the act of leaving.

cue: Your toddler is crying at the nursery door as you hand her over, and you have to turn and go to work anyway.

ctx.s: 泣[な]いている子供[こども]を置[お]いて、{後[うし]ろ髪[がみ]を引[ひ]かれる}思[おも]いで会社[かいしゃ]へ向[む]かった。

ctx.en: "Are you going already?" "Yes, I hate to leave, but I've got an early start tomorrow."

bad.en: (meant: I finally quit that awful job and feel so relieved)
bad.why: It is reluctance to leave something you care about. Relief at getting away is seisei suru or hotto suru.

bad.en: (meant: I still regret what I said yesterday)
bad.why: It is about the pull felt when leaving a person or place, not regret over a past mistake. Say kuyande iru.
